newsitem.title: USA: U.S. excuses Italian firm from Cuba sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. excuses Italian firm from Cuba sanctions.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday excused Italian telecommunications company STET International from penalties under the Helms-Burton law after the firm struck a deal with America's ITT Corp. over telephone holdings in Cuba.

The U.S. State Department said STET paid ITT an undisclosed sum for a free hand in the Cuban telephone system, which ITT built and operated until it was seized by communist authorities after the 1959 revolution in Cuba.
Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the deal, valid for 10 years, exonerated the Italian company from liability under Helms-Burton over its holding in Cuban telecommunications company ETECSA.

"The department has, therefore, terminated without adverse action the investigation which had been ongoing related to STET International's and its affiliates' use of ITT's confiscated property in Cuba," Burns said in a written statement.

A section of the Helms-Burton law, passed in 1996, provides for senior executives of companies deemed to be "trafficking" in property seized from U.S. nationals in Cuba to be barred from the United States.

Burns said the settlement "sends a clear signal to foreign companies in Cuba using confiscated U.S. property that they will either have to reach agreement with U.S. national claimants ... or face visa denial/exclusion sanctions."
The agreement was also hailed by Republican Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and one of the sponsors of the law.
"This deal should serve as a warning to anyone considering investing in Cuba: the price of doing business in (Cuban President Fidel) Castro's tropical gulag has just gone up," he said in a statement.

The Cuban American National Foundation, an influential emigre group, called the deal a victory but said it still opposed STET's presence in Cuba, "subsidizing tyranny and profiting from the misery of the Cuban people."
Burns said the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control had reviewed the STET-ITT agreement and issued a license to ITT to authorize it to implement the accord.

The agreement over STET meant the United States has sanctioned two foreign companies under the so-called Title Four of Helms-Burton -- Canadian mining group Sherritt International Corp and Mexican telecommunications firm Grupo Domos.
Grupo Domos invested along with STET in ETECSA, holding a larger share, but the Mexicans pulled out earlier this year, leading the Italian firm to raise its stake.

Another section of Helms-Burton, Title Three, allows U.S. nationals to sue foreign firms using their confiscated property in Cuba, but has been waived three times by President Bill Clinton, most recently last week.

The administration's waivers of Title Three and limited application of Title Four have angered opponents of Castro's government, including Helms, who charge that Clinton is colluding with the European Union, which opposes Helms-Burton.
Helms's statement on Wednesday said administration officials had taken no action against STET for 13 months and the deal with ITT "in no way justifies their failure to enforce the law."
